variations.name: Conventional & run-of-river hydropower (incl. modernization/uprating)
variations.description: Flowing river water, impounded behind dams or diverted run-of-river, spins turbines; at roughly 1,400 GW installed it is the world's largest renewable electricity source, and re-powering 50+ year-old fleets adds clean capacity and grid flexibility without building new dams.

companies.name: Voith Hydro
companies.what: Top-3 global hydro OEM supplying turbines, generators and full-plant modernization/uprating packages for utility fleets.
companies.signal: Century-old hydro franchise; modernization/refurbishment is a core dedicated business line across Europe, Americas, Asia.

companies.name: Andritz Hydro
companies.what: Austrian OEM with one of the largest installed turbine bases worldwide; 'from water-to-wire' new builds plus a large refurbishment and service business.
companies.signal: Top-3 hydro OEM; presented major modernization and pumped-storage projects alongside Voith at Volta-X 2025.

companies.name: GE Vernova (Hydro Power)
companies.what: Supplies large Francis/Kaplan and pumped-storage equipment and uprates a major share of the global installed hydro fleet.
companies.signal: NYSE-listed since 2024 spin-off; hydro sits in its Power segment with record 2025 orders companywide.

companies.name: Brookfield Renewable
companies.what: One of the largest non-utility hydro owner-operators (~8 GW), monetizing 24/7 carbon-free hydro through corporate offtakes.
companies.signal: July 2025: ~$3B framework agreement with Google for up to 3,000 MW of US hydropower (first tranche in PJM).

companies.name: Statkraft
companies.what: Europe's largest renewable generator, hydro-dominated, using machine-learning plant optimization to squeeze more output from existing assets.
companies.signal: Reported ~20% capacity boosts across 12 plants via ML optimization.

companies.name: Innergex Renewable Energy
companies.what: Independent power producer with a large run-of-river hydro fleet (British Columbia, Quebec, Chile, France) within a 4.7 GW renewables portfolio.
companies.signal: Taken private by pension giant CDPQ for ~C$10B (announced Feb 2025, closed July 2025) at a 58% premium — institutional capital paying up for run-of-river hydro.

variations.name: Small & modular hydro (low-head, fish-safe turbines)
variations.description: Compact, standardized turbines — including fish-safe runners, submersible units and vortex/screw designs — extract power from low dams, locks, weirs and conduits, unlocking the tens of GW sitting at existing non-powered dams without new impoundments.

companies.name: Natel Energy
companies.what: FishSafe Restoration Hydro Turbine with thick blunt-edged blades that lets fish pass through the runner alive (98-100% demonstrated survival) at up to 94% efficiency.
companies.signal: ~$9M in DOE WPTO funding across seven programs; 2025 feasibility study for NYPA to retrofit the St. Lawrence-FDR project; commercial units in US and Europe.

companies.name: Rye Development
companies.what: Develops low-impact, low-head hydro plants on existing US Army Corps locks and dams (Ohio, Allegheny, Monongahela rivers).
companies.signal: Constructing at Emsworth, Charleroi and Allegheny L/D 2 with a dozen-plus project offtake pipeline; separately won $81M DOE award for pumped storage.

companies.name: Turbulent
companies.what: Belgian maker of 15-100 kW gravitational vortex micro-hydro plants for sites with under 3 m of head, built modularly for off-grid and rural use.
companies.signal: Installations across Chile, Indonesia, the Philippines and Europe; equity-crowdfunded and distributor-driven growth.

companies.name: Voith Hydro (StreamDiver)
companies.what: Plug-and-play sealed submersible turbine product line for very low-head sites and existing weirs, requiring no powerhouse.
companies.signal: Commercial product with deployments in Europe and North America, sold as a standardized small-hydro module.

companies.name: Andritz (Compact Hydro)
companies.what: Standardized 'Compact Hydro' equipment line for small plants up to ~30 MW, cutting engineering cost via series production.
companies.signal: Thousands of compact units delivered globally as part of the world's largest small-hydro equipment business.

variations.white_space: Per-kW costs and site-specific civil works keep small hydro above solar+storage in most markets; the opening is standardization plus retrofit of the ~90,000 US non-powered dams under streamlined FERC licensing, where fish-safe turbines (Natel) collapse the cost of environmental compliance.

variations.name: Hydrokinetic river & canal turbines
variations.description: Submerged turbines harvest kinetic energy from free-flowing rivers and irrigation canals with no dam at all; output per unit is small but highly predictable, making it ideal for displacing diesel in remote communities and monetizing existing canal infrastructure.

companies.name: ORPC (Ocean Renewable Power Company)
companies.what: RivGen cross-flow river turbines integrated with microgrid controls and storage to displace diesel in remote villages.
companies.signal: Two RivGen units have powered Igiugig, Alaska since 2019/2023 — the longest-operating hydrokinetic project in the Americas; multi-program DOE backing.

companies.name: Emrgy
companies.what: Drop-in modular hydrokinetic turbines for irrigation canals, partnering with water districts to generate from existing flows and drops.
companies.signal: $18.4M raise (2023) plus $3.6M ARPA-E SHARKS award; arrays deployed in US irrigation districts (Denver, California).

companies.name: Idénergie
companies.what: Montreal maker of a portable ~500 W Darrieus river turbine producing up to 12 kWh/day for off-grid cabins and remote homes.
companies.signal: Consumer product sold since ~2016, but little visible company activity since 2019.

companies.name: Smart Hydro Power
companies.what: German supplier of floating 5 kW hydrokinetic turbines and hybrid kits for rural electrification in Peru, India and elsewhere.
companies.signal: Pioneered floating river turbines in the 2010s; minimal recent news or funding activity.

variations.white_space: Slow rivers carry little extractable energy density and debris/ice drive O&M costs, so per-kWh economics lose to solar+storage almost everywhere; the credible wedges are Arctic and remote diesel-dependent communities (ORPC's niche, with diesel at $0.50+/kWh) and irrigation canals where interconnection, water rights and civil works already exist (Emrgy's niche) — two startups effectively own these openings today.

variations.name: Tidal stream turbines (seabed, floating, kite)
variations.description: Underwater turbines — bottom-mounted, hung from floating platforms, or flown on subsea kites — convert fast, astronomically predictable tidal currents into electricity, providing forecastable renewable power that complements variable wind and solar.

companies.name: Proteus Marine Renewables
companies.what: Builds megawatt-class seabed turbines (the AR series inherited from SIMEC Atlantis), the workhorse machines at MeyGen and in Japan.
companies.signal: Installed a 1.1 MW turbine in Japan's Naru Strait (Feb 2025); upgraded 1.5 MW unit revenue-generating at MeyGen; SKF partnership to deliver a minimum 59 MW MeyGen expansion.

companies.name: SAE Renewables
companies.what: AIM-listed owner-operator of MeyGen in Scotland's Pentland Firth, the world's largest tidal stream array.
companies.signal: MeyGen has produced 84+ GWh, a world record; awarded a further 9 MW CfD in AR6 (Sept 2024) for delivery 2028/29.

companies.name: Orbital Marine Power
companies.what: Floating tidal platform (O2, 2 MW — the world's most powerful tidal turbine) with retractable legs for cheap vessel-free maintenance.
companies.signal: O2 grid-connected at EMEC since 2021; 17 MW CfD portfolio after AR7 (Feb 2026); £7M round closed Dec 2025; next-gen 2.4 MW O2-X received Lloyd's IECRE feasibility statement.

companies.name: Minesto
companies.what: Subsea 'kite' (Dragon 12) that flies figure-eights to multiply effective flow speed, enabling power from low-velocity tidal sites others can't use.
companies.signal: Nasdaq First North-listed; 1.2 MW Dragon 12 grid-connected in the Faroe Islands May 2025 with +25% output from a longer tether; >€40M cumulative EU funding; microgrid demo with Swedish Energy Agency.

companies.name: Nova Innovation
companies.what: Direct-drive seabed turbines; built the world's first offshore tidal array (Bluemull Sound, Shetland, 2016).
companies.signal: Won 6 MW of CfDs in AR6 (2024) for EMEC deployment, but diversified into floating solar via the AquaGen365 JV with RSK (2024) — a hedge signaling tidal revenue strain.

companies.name: HydroQuest
companies.what: French vertical-axis ducted tidal turbines; leading FloWatt, the 17 MW pilot farm at Raz Blanchard, Normandy.
companies.signal: €65M French state support plus revenue support; 72 composite blades ordered from Loiretech in early 2025; commissioning targeted 2028.

companies.name: Verdant Power
companies.what: Axial-flow turbines on a TriFrame mount, proven at the NYC East River RITE site (Gen5, 2020-21, powering Con Edison's grid).
companies.signal: Small (~16-person) team; Verdant Isles JV holds a 4.9 MW UK CfD for 2027/28 off Anglesey; research collaboration with Stony Brook running into 2026.

companies.name: Sustainable Marine Energy
companies.what: Floating PLAT-I tidal platform; delivered Canada's first floating tidal power to the Nova Scotia grid in the Bay of Fundy.
companies.signal: Withdrew its 9 MW Pempa'q project blaming an opaque DFO permitting process, then entered administration in August 2023 — a regulatory-risk cautionary tale.

variations.name: Tidal range, barrages & lagoons
variations.description: Dams or artificial lagoons across high-tide-range estuaries impound seawater and release it through bulb turbines, delivering utility-scale, century-lifetime, perfectly predictable generation — at multi-billion upfront cost and with estuarine ecosystem impacts.

companies.name: EDF
companies.what: Operates the 240 MW La Rance barrage in Brittany, the world's longest-running tidal power station, since 1966.
companies.signal: Six decades of commercial operation proving century-scale asset life for tidal range.

companies.name: K-water (Korea Water Resources Corp)
companies.what: Operates the 254 MW Sihwa Lake plant (2011), the world's largest tidal power station, built into an existing seawall.
companies.signal: One of only two large tidal range plants operating worldwide; piggybacked on existing infrastructure to manage cost.

companies.name: Tidal Lagoon Power
companies.what: Developed the 320 MW Swansea Bay 'pathfinder' tidal lagoon, the UK's flagship private tidal-range venture.
companies.signal: Collapsed after the UK government rejected its CfD in 2018 on value-for-money grounds — the sector's defining failure.

companies.name: Mersey Tidal Power (Liverpool City Region Combined Authority)
companies.what: Publicly led ~£3.5bn barrage/lagoon scheme on the Mersey, the UK's most advanced tidal range project in the planning pipeline.
companies.signal: Combined Authority approved progression in Sept 2024; registered with the Planning Inspectorate for DCO consenting.

variations.white_space: The resource is enormous and perfectly predictable (the Severn alone could supply ~7% of UK electricity), but no private balance sheet can carry multi-billion, 120-year assets with 20+ year paybacks plus habitats-directive litigation — which is why only two large plants exist and the lone venture-backed attempt (Swansea) died. The Severn Estuary Commission (March 2025) recommended a government-enabled demonstration lagoon over any barrage; the opening is for sovereign/pension capital and EPC consortia under regulated-asset-base style financing, not startups.

variations.name: Wave energy converters (point absorber, OWC, attenuator, overtopping)
variations.description: Devices spanning point absorbers, oscillating water columns, hinged flaps/attenuators and overtopping designs convert wave motion into electricity; the global resource is vast and winter-peaking, complementing solar, but survivability in storms has historically destroyed both devices and companies.

companies.name: CorPower Ocean
companies.what: Swedish point absorber with WaveSpring phase control that amplifies motion in normal seas and detunes to survive storms, claiming ~5x energy per ton.
companies.signal: C4 grid-connected at Aguçadoura, Portugal; €32M Series B1 plus up to €17.5M EIC (Feb 2025); leading the €30M POWER-Farm EU toward a 10 MW farm; EMEC berth signed May 2025.

companies.name: Eco Wave Power
companies.what: Nasdaq-listed (WAVE) developer of breakwater/jetty-mounted floaters with all conversion equipment onshore, slashing marine installation and O&M cost.
companies.signal: Launched the first US onshore wave project at the Port of Los Angeles (100 kW, with AltaSea and Shell MRE) in Sept 2025; grid-connected EWP-EDF One in Israel; raised $3M toward a 20 MW commercial plant.

companies.name: AW-Energy
companies.what: Finnish maker of the WaveRoller, a seabed-hinged oscillating flap (350 kW) operating in the nearshore surge zone off Peniche, Portugal.
companies.signal: USD 19.1M revenue in 2024 from deployments and licensing; ONDEP Horizon Europe project will deploy a four-device array at Peniche.

companies.name: Carnegie Clean Energy
companies.what: ASX-listed developer of CETO, a fully submerged point absorber that avoids storm loading by sitting beneath the surface.
companies.signal: Advancing CETO through the EuropeWave ACHIEVE program toward deployment at BiMEP, Spain; operates the Garden Island wave/solar microgrid in Western Australia.

companies.name: Ocean Power Technologies
companies.what: NYSE-listed (OPTT) maker of the PB3 PowerBuoy for autonomous offshore power; strategically pivoted from utility-scale wave power to maritime security, sensors and WAM-V unmanned surface vessels.
companies.signal: Decades-listed survivor whose pivot away from grid-scale wave power is itself market evidence; recurring defense and offshore-monitoring contracts.

companies.name: Mocean Energy
companies.what: Scottish hinged-raft attenuator (Blue X/Blue Horizon) targeting near-term revenue powering subsea oil & gas and offshore equipment with Verlume subsea batteries.
companies.signal: Completed multi-phase Renewables for Subsea Power demos with industry partners (Harbour Energy, Serica, et al.) off Orkney.

companies.name: CalWave Power Technologies
companies.what: Fully submerged xWave pressure-differential absorber that operates beneath the surface for storm survivability.
companies.signal: Completed a 10-month open-water pilot off San Diego with 99% uptime; DOE-backed deployment planned at the PacWave South test site.

companies.name: Oscilla Power
companies.what: Triton multi-mode point absorber with a ring-shaped reaction hull; the 100 kW Triton-C was deployed at the US Navy's WETS site in Hawaii.
companies.signal: DOE and Navy-supported; one of the few US devices to reach grid-connected ocean testing.

companies.name: Wello Oy
companies.what: Finnish developer of the Penguin rotating-eccentric-mass converter with all moving parts sealed inside the hull.
companies.signal: Filed for bankruptcy in Feb 2023 after two full-scale Penguins failed at sea (last off Spain, 2021); IP and team picked up by Holvi Oy.

companies.name: Wave Swell Energy
companies.what: Australian oscillating water column (UniWave200) with a simplified one-way turbine, validated on the King Island grid in Tasmania.
companies.signal: 200 kW unit ran 2021-22 then was decommissioned and removed (Mar 2023); opened an investment round afterward but little public progress since.

variations.name: Ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC)
variations.description: Exploits the 20-25°C temperature difference between warm tropical surface water and 4°C deep ocean water to run a closed Rankine cycle around the clock — thermodynamically inefficient but tapping an enormous baseload resource best matched to island grids paying diesel prices.

companies.name: Makai Ocean Engineering
companies.what: Hawaii engineering firm with 40+ years in OTEC; operates one of the world's only grid-connected OTEC plants (105 kW at NELHA) and builds Thin-Foil Heat Exchangers attacking OTEC's largest cost component.
companies.signal: 2025 MoU to integrate its TFHX into Global OTEC's modular 500 kW Power Module scalable to 50 MW.

companies.name: Global OTEC
companies.what: UK startup commercializing floating OTEC barges for island states — the 1.5 MW 'Dominique' for São Tomé and Príncipe, upscalable to 10 MW.
companies.signal: Lloyd's Register Approval in Principle; UNIDO-supported ESIA underway; Horizon Europe/UKRI-funded PLOTEC storm-resilient platform; Makai heat-exchanger partnership (2025).

companies.name: Bluerise
companies.what: Dutch OTEC and seawater air-conditioning pioneer (Curaçao projects) spun out of TU Delft.
companies.signal: Acquired by offshore contractor Allseas (2019), which absorbed the technology to develop OTEC at offshore-industry scale.

companies.name: Ocean Thermal Energy Corporation (OTE)
companies.what: Long-running US developer of OTEC and SWAC projects (Bahamas resorts), publicly framing the sector's 'Innovation Valley of Death.'
companies.signal: States a first 5-10 MW plant needs $200-300M that no one has funded; little visible project construction.

variations.white_space: Physics caps OTEC at ~3-4% thermal efficiency from a ~22°C delta, so gigantic water flows, kilometer-scale cold-water pipes and heat-exchanger area dominate cost — no plant above 1 MW has ever run, and the $200-300M first commercial unit has no natural funder. The opening: small island states burning diesel at $0.25-0.40/kWh, with desalination and seawater air-conditioning co-products, plus defense interest in island bases; a verified heat-exchanger/cold-pipe cost breakthrough (e.g., Makai's TFHX in Global OTEC's barge) is the unlock, leaving the field to essentially two credible players.

variations.name: Salinity-gradient / osmotic power
variations.description: Mixing fresh and salt water releases free energy ('blue energy') that membranes capture via reverse electrodialysis or pressure-retarded osmosis at estuaries, salt caverns and desalination outfalls — a 24/7, weather-independent resource estimated in the thousands of TWh per year.

companies.name: Sweetch Energy
companies.what: French CNRS spin-off whose INOD nanofluidic electrodes/membranes deliver order-of-magnitude higher power density for reverse electrodialysis at river mouths.
companies.signal: ~€50M raised (Crédit Mutuel Impact, EDF Pulse, CNR, EIC); OsmoRhône 1 pilot operating at the Rhône delta with CNR since end-2024; WEF Technology Pioneer 2025; targets ~500 MW Rhône potential.

companies.name: SaltPower
companies.what: Danish company running pressure-retarded osmosis on saturated salt-cavern brine, whose extreme gradient (10x seawater) sidesteps the power-density problem that killed estuary PRO.
companies.signal: ~100 kW commercial unit operating at a Nobian salt site; EU Horizon 2020 scale-up project; founded 2015.

companies.name: REDstack
companies.what: Dutch reverse-electrodialysis developer operating the 'Blue Energy' pilot on the Afsluitdijk mixing Wadden Sea and IJsselmeer water since 2014.
companies.signal: ~€5M Waddenfonds grant for scale-up; exploring green hydrogen co-production at the plant.

companies.name: Statkraft
companies.what: Built the world's first pressure-retarded-osmosis prototype plant (Tofte, Norway, 2009) — then shut the program down circa 2013-14 when membrane power density made costs hopeless.
companies.signal: The sector's defining cautionary tale: an incumbent with cheap capital exited because membranes delivered ~1 W/m² against a ~5 W/m² breakeven.

variations.white_space: Classical membranes produce under 1-3 W/m² versus a ~5 W/m² economic threshold — that physics killed Statkraft's pioneer plant and kept the field empty for a decade. New nanomaterial electrodes (Sweetch) and extreme-gradient siting (SaltPower's saturated brines) reopen it; the white space is co-location with desalination outfalls and salt/chlor-alkali industries where the gradient is free and water pretreatment already exists — only ~3 credible companies worldwide are pursuing a resource theoretically worth a fifth of global electricity.
